newsitem.title: GERMANY: German police say looted Russian treasure found.
newsitem.headline: German police say looted Russian treasure found.

text.p: German police said on Wednesday they had found a mosaic they were confident belonged to the Amber Chamber, a tsarist treasure stolen by Nazi troops in World War Two and missing since 1945.
The presumed find follows an embarrassing episode last year when police in Munich were tricked into hunting down fragments of the priceless treasure that later turned out to be fake.

Police in Potsdam said on Wednesday they had discovered a mosaic which initial investigations had confirmed belonged to the chamber, an assembly of amber wall panels and furniture presented to the tsars by Prussia in 1712.
They said the mosaic had been traced to a notary in Bremen who had been given the artwork for safe-keeping. A definitive verification of the piece by art historians was now being arranged, they said.

The small mosaic picture, depicting two couples relaxing in a garden landscape, was screened on the main evening news programme of the Vox commercial television channel, which said reporters affiliated to it had helped police track it down.
The television channel said in its report that Russian President Boris Yeltsin was being informed of the find.
The Amber Chamber was dismantled and removed from an imperial palace near St Petersburg, then Leningrad, by German troops in 1941.
It was last seen in the German city of Koenigsberg, now Kaliningrad in Russia, just before the German retreat in 1945. The chamber tops Russia's list of missing treasures looted by the Nazis.

Bavarian police thought they were on the trail of the treasure last May when a hoax television film claiming that the chamber had been found and was being shipped across Germany was picked up as a top news story by two television stations.
Police rushed to intercept the shipment on a highway outside Munich, only to find the supposed artwork was a fake made for a TV spoof programme called "Can You Take a Joke?"
The treasure has been the object of frequent searches in Germany, and experts have combed cellars, caverns and lakes around Kaliningrad for decades searching for the panels.
In 1991-92, two eastern German towns excavated old Third Reich bunkers in vain after reports that the panels were buried there.
